2. Project report

2.1 Problem definition

Task. Supervised 10-class classification of garment images (Fashion-MNIST), used as a vehicle to study the softmax-regression model: how faithfully does minimising the convex cross-entropy surrogate track the quantities we actually care about (0-1 error, cost-weighted error, calibration), and which mechanisms control the gaps?

Training phaseDeployment phase
InputX ∈ ℝn×784, n = 50,000. Row = a 28×28 greyscale catalogue image flattened row-major, raw integers 0…255 (0 = background). Pre-processing x̃ = (x/255 − μ)/σ with μ ∈ ℝ784 the per-pixel training mean and σ = 0.295 one global training std (centred, front-view, background-removed product photos; not photos in the wild). One 28×28 uint8 image through the same frozen (μ, σ). Out of scope: colour, rotated, cluttered images.
Output / labely ∈ {0..9} (T-shirt, Trouser, Pullover, Dress, Coat, Sandal, Shirt, Sneaker, Bag, Ankle boot) as one-hot ey; ≈ 5,000 per class. Probability vector q ∈ Δ9 (qk ≥ 0, Σqk = 1) and the decision ŷ = argmaxk qk (or the minimum-expected-cost class).
Compared viaq vs ey through cross-entropy (convex surrogate).ŷ vs truth through the task objective: 0-1 error / cost-weighted error; q through calibration (ECE).

Splits. 60,000 official training images → 50,000 train / 10,000 validation (seeded random split); the official 10,000 test images are used once, after all choices are frozen.

Challenges. (i) Four upper-body classes (T-shirt/Shirt/Pullover/Coat) are visually near-identical, so a linear model cannot reach low error; (ii) pixel correlation ⇒ ill-conditioned optimisation (κ ≤ 1.1e+04); (iii) softmax is over-parameterised (shift invariance) ⇒ convex but not strictly convex; (iv) the training loss is not the task objective.

Motivation and historical perspective

Softmax regression is the simplest model in which every ingredient of modern ML is visible and analysable: a hypothesis space, an information-theoretic loss, a convex optimisation problem, a norm-based generalisation bound, and a probabilistic output. The last layer of nearly every deep classifier is a softmax regression, so understanding it exactly transfers to deep networks. History: Berkson (1944) introduced the logit; Cox (1958) formalised logistic regression; the multinomial form is Theil (1969) / McFadden (1974); Rosenblatt's perceptron (1958) gave a linear classifier without probabilities; Jaynes' maximum-entropy principle (1957) shows softmax regression is exactly the max-entropy distribution matching empirical feature moments (Berger et al. 1996 for NLP); Bridle (1990) named “softmax”. Learning theory then asked why minimising a convex surrogate is legitimate: Zhang (2004) and Bartlett–Jordan–McAuliffe (2006) proved calibration/consistency of cross-entropy — but only for unrestricted function classes and infinite data; Bartlett–Mendelson (2002) and Kakade–Sridharan–Tewari (2008) gave norm-based bounds ∝ BR/√n for linear predictors; Soudry et al. (2018) showed gradient descent on separable data has an implicit bias to the max-margin solution with ‖W‖ growing only like log t; Guo et al. (2017) documented mis-calibration of CE-trained models; Zhang & Sabuncu (2018) and Ghosh et al. (2017) studied bounded losses robust to label noise. Why ML rather than rules: no closed-form rule maps 784 correlated intensities to “Coat” vs “Shirt”, while 60k i.i.d. labelled examples from a stable catalogue distribution are available — the conditions that justify empirical risk minimisation. Why linear rather than a CNN: the linear model is the object of study: convex (optimisation separable from modelling), capacity controlled by ‖W‖ (theory testable), and its residual error quantifies what non-linear features add.

Research question and hypotheses

  • H1 (capacity): the generalisation gap is governed by ‖W‖FR/√n, not by the number of parameters (7,850).
  • H2 (loss ≠ objective): CE is more sensitive than 0-1 error to over-fitting and to rescaling of logits; the mismatch is measurable and repairable (temperature scaling).
  • H3 (optimisation as regulariser): with λ = 0 on separable data the loss is never minimised: ‖W‖ ∝ log t and the margin grows.
  • H4 (customised loss): under symmetric label noise a bounded re-weighted CE (generalised CE) is more robust than CE at no cost on clean data.

2.2 Machine-learning approach

Model and justification

Hypothesis space: q(x;W,b) = softmax(Wᵀx + b), W ∈ ℝ784×10, b ∈ ℝ10 (7,850 parameters). Linear log-odds is the exponential-family/GLM choice, equals the max-entropy distribution with matching feature moments, and has a convex negative log-likelihood. Shift invariance softmax(z + c1) = softmax(z) creates 785 flat directions of the unregularised loss (verified numerically below); the L2 penalty removes them.

Loss and gradient. ℓCE(z,y) = −log qy = H(ey, q) = KL(ey‖q) (since H(ey) = 0), so ERM = maximum likelihood. ∂ℓ/∂z = q − ey, hence ∇WJ = Xᵀ(Q−Y)/n + λW, ∇bJ = 1ᵀ(Q−Y)/n with J = mean ℓ + (λ/2)‖W‖²F (bias unpenalised). At a λ = 0 optimum Xᵀ(Q − Y) = 0 (moment matching). The Hessian (1/n)Σ(diag qi − qiqiᵀ) ⊗ x̃ix̃iᵀ is PSD (convex) and ⪯ L·I with L = ½λmax(X̃ᵀX̃/n) + λ, giving a principled step 1/L and κ ≤ L/λ.

Customised component. Generalised cross-entropy ℓq = (1 − qyq)/q (→ CE as q → 0, = MAE at q = 1). I derived ∂ℓq/∂zj = qyq(qj − 1[j=y]) — CE's gradient re-weighted by qyq, so likely-mislabelled points are down-weighted — and verified it by finite differences.

Training procedure and hyper-parameters

ItemSetting (reason)
Pre-processing/255, per-pixel train mean, one global train std (keeps geometry; per-pixel std would amplify near-constant border pixels)
RegularisationL2 on W; λ ∈ {1e-6,…,1e-1} chosen by 5-fold CV on a 20k subset; λ* = 0.01
Main solverown L-BFGS, m = 10, Armijo c₁ = 1e-4, up to 800 iterations on the final fit (converged solutions needed so early stopping does not confound λ)
GD / momentumη = 1/L (L = 113.4 computed from data); heavy-ball β = 0.9
Adamβ₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.999, ε = 1e-8; lr 1e-2 (convergence comparison), 3e-3 (over-fitting study), 2e-3 with batch 64 (noise study)
SeedsSEED = 2025 (split), fixed seeds per experiment; 5 folds / 5 seeds / 2 subsets for ± values

Evaluation metrics and relevance

0-1 error — the task objective (classes balanced, so accuracy is not misleading); macro-F1 + per-class P/R/F1 + confusion matrix — class-specific failures hidden by the mean; cross-entropy — the training loss, a proper scoring rule; Brier — second bounded proper score; ECE (15 bins) — whether stated confidence matches accuracy. Baselines: majority class, nearest-class-mean. Uncertainty: fold std, seed std and bootstrap 95 % CI. The ideal comparison (0-1 loss) is not used for training because it is piecewise constant (zero gradient a.e.) and NP-hard to minimise for linear classes; it is measured on validation/test instead.

2.4 Discussion

Findings and implications

  • Task performance. 15.95% test error (CI [15.14%, 16.66%]) vs 90 % chance and 32 % for a no-training linear baseline; macro-F1 0.839. Errors are systematic: the upper-body classes, especially Shirt (F1 0.59).
  • H1 supported (as association). The plug-in complexity ‖Ŵ‖FR/√n predicts the gap (ρ = 0.99 for CE) although the parameter count is constant; parameter count is not what controls generalisation here. This tests the shape, not the bound's constants (which are loose).
  • H2 supported. CE exaggerates over-fitting (+61% vs +15% for error) and a single scalar T changes test CE 24× with zero change in any decision. A model comparison on CE alone can therefore mislead; we need decision metrics and a calibration check. Confident mistakes dominate the loss (5 % of points = 36.1%) while 27.6% of errors are almost free for the loss — the disagreement goes both ways.
  • H3 supported. With λ = 0 the optimum is not attained; ‖W‖ grows like log t (R² = 0.999). The stopping time is a hidden regulariser, which is why λ must be chosen with converged solvers (the reason for implementing L-BFGS).
  • H4 supported under stated conditions. 40 % symmetric noise: GCE(0.7) 21.8%–22.7% vs CE 34.9%–40.5%; clean-label cost nil. At λ = 1e-3 GCE is even better on clean data (18.4 % vs 20.1 %), which I attribute to CE over-fitting n = 3000 rather than to GCE being intrinsically better.
  • Cost-aware decisions: small effect. The Bayes-risk rule lowers the assumed expected cost by ≈ 0–3.5 % and raises 0-1 error by 0.02–0.25 pp: the two objectives genuinely differ, but this model's posteriors are rarely ambiguous in a way that changes many decisions.
  • Optimisation. κ ≈ 10⁴: GD at 1/L is very slow; Adam and especially L-BFGS handle the conditioning. 1/L is a safe, not optimal, step (GD still converges at 8/L).

Limitations

(1) Linear hypothesis space: ≈ 4 pp behind a small MLP — approximation error dominates; (2) single dataset and single train/validation split for the final model (CV covers λ only; the bootstrap CI reflects test-set sampling); (3) H1 is tested via a plug-in proxy with 2 seeds — association, not proof; (4) the cost matrix is assumed; (5) GCE experiments: n = 3000, symmetric noise, final iterates, non-convex objective; (6) the over-fitting demonstration is one small-n regime; (7) std estimates from 5 folds/seeds are themselves noisy; (8) tuning of Adam learning rates was coarse.

Potential improvements / future work

Architecture: random-feature/kernel or convolutional features (texture and sleeve-length cues for Shirt vs T-shirt). Algorithmic: (a) a calibration- or cost-aware training objective instead of post-hoc repair; (b) noise-transition-matrix correction for class-dependent label noise (the most confident errors look like ambiguous labels); (c) compare the log t drift against an explicit multi-class hard-margin SVM; (d) PCA whitening / pre-conditioning to reduce κ; (e) estimate the bound's constants through Monte-Carlo empirical Rademacher complexity to test H1 quantitatively.

3.1 Challenges and solutions

#Challenge (what I observed)Diagnosis and solution
1Gradient check failed my 1e-6 threshold (1.2·10⁻⁶ relative error for CE).Suspected a bug, but the error was at the level of finite-difference truncation/round-off (h = 1e-6). With h = 1e-5 errors were 7.7·10⁻⁷ (CE) and 1.1·10⁻⁷ (GCE) and the independent Hessian-vs-gradient test agreed to 4·10⁻¹¹, so I relaxed the threshold to 1e-5 and documented why.
2With λ = 1e-3 my L-BFGS reference and scikit-learn disagreed (objective 2.7·10⁻⁴; probabilities up to 0.26); neither hit its tolerance.Not a correctness bug but ill-conditioning (κ ≤ 10⁴–10⁵) and non-convergence. Moved the comparison to λ = 1e-2, 1500 iterations; agreement became 6·10⁻¹³. Lesson: a “reference optimum” must itself be verified converged (‖∇J‖ = 2·10⁻⁷).
3Naive Update beat gradient descent in my first plot.The comparison was unfair (GD η = 0.01 untuned; equal iterations but 100× the compute for random search). Re-ran with η = 1/L and an x-axis in forward-pass equivalents.
4My first loss-vs-error “decoupling” experiment (n = 5,000) was weak: val CE rose only ≈ 2.6 %.Re-ran at n = 2,000 (lr 3e-3) and, importantly, changed the claim from “decoupled” to “CE exaggerates over-fitting”; the stronger demonstration is temperature scaling, where the decisions are provably identical.
5Fitted temperature of the over-fit model sat on my grid boundary (T = 5).Extended the grid to [0.2, 100]; optimum T = 44.5 (CE 16.1 → 0.66).
6GCE beat CE even on clean labels at λ = 1e-3, suspicious for a claim about robustness.Suspected a regularisation confound; ran both losses on a matched λ grid. The clean-data gap shrinks at λ = 1e-2 while the 40 %-noise gap persists, so I report the robustness claim and flag the clean-data difference as over-fitting.
7Cost-sensitive decisions gave only a small gain.I did not tune the assumed cost matrix to enlarge the effect; I added a sensitivity analysis over cin and reported the modest result.
8Numerical stability and runtime: naive softmax overflows; the full notebook took ≈ 15 min.Log-sum-exp shift (checked with logits × 1000); reduced the MLP epochs, seeds at large n and CV subset size; cached data download with an OpenML fallback.

Anticipated questions (short answers)

  • Why is ∂ℓ/∂z = q − ey? ℓ = −zy + log Σezj; the derivative of the log-sum-exp is softmax.
  • Why 785 zero eigenvalues of the Hessian? Shift invariance: adding v to every class column leaves q unchanged, so those directions have zero curvature (verified: d+1 zero eigenvalues on a small problem).
  • Why L-BFGS and not Adam for CV? I need converged solutions; otherwise the stopping time regularises and confounds λ. Adam is shown for conditioning comparison.
  • Why is 1/L safe but GD works at 8/L? L uses λmax(diag q − qqᵀ) ≤ ½, attained only for two-class ties; near the optimum most points are confident so curvature is far smaller.
  • Why does GCE help? Its gradient is CE's times qyq, so points the model finds very unlikely (candidate mislabels) get little weight.
  • Does temperature scaling change accuracy? No: argmax(z/T) = argmax(z).
  • Is the generalisation bound verified? No — only its shape (association with a plug-in proxy); constants are unknown/loose.
  • I don't know… is acceptable: state what you would check (the notebook cell, a reference).
